title: Trump: Young Don Jr: My dad loves his money, and that's it
description_short: Trump: Young Don Jr: My dad loves his money, and that's it
description_medium: Vanity Fair’s September 1990 feature “After the Gold Rush” described the deteriorating relationship between Donald and Ivana Trump. description_long:
Vanity Fair’s September 1990 feature “After the Gold Rush” examined the deteriorating relationship between Donald and Ivana Trump. Friends interviewed for the article recalled a conversation earlier that year in which 12-year-old Donald Trump Jr. challenged his father, asking how he could claim to love his children and saying, “You just love your money.” The exact date of the exchange was not established. The article also recalled that Trump’s mother, Mary, asked Ivana what kind of son she had created.

The account came from people close to Ivana who spoke with Vanity Fair; it was not a recording or a direct interview with Trump Jr. The anecdote appeared within a broader feature about the couple’s strained relationship and public separation. It offers a secondhand glimpse into the family tensions described by people around them, but does not independently verify the private conversation or establish when it took place.

Before the decision, Trump attorney Marc Kasowitz had donated $25,000 to Vance’s campaign; Vance later refunded it. Kasowitz subsequently donated again. description_long:
In August 2012, Manhattan District Attorney Cyrus Vance dropped felony fraud charges against Ivanka Trump and Donald Trump Jr. concerning alleged misstatements about Trump SoHo condominium values. Their lawyer, Marc Kasowitz, had donated $25,000 to Vance before the decision. Vance returned the contribution, saying he wanted to prevent speculation; Kasowitz later donated another $50,000. People quoted in reporting said Kasowitz later described the case as dangerous and said it was remarkable he had gotten the Trump children out of it. Kasowitz denied making those remarks.

The sequence drew scrutiny because a campaign donor’s clients benefited from a prosecutorial decision involving the family of a prominent political figure. The donations and dismissal prompted questions about prosecutorial discretion, but the available facts do not establish a quid pro quo or show that the contributions influenced Vance. No finding of bribery or prosecutorial misconduct is described.

title: Donald Trump threatens to send police to polling places, voter intimidation
description_short: Donald Trump threatens to send police to polling places, voter intimidation
description_medium: In an August 20, 2020 Fox News interview, Donald Trump said he hoped to have sheriffs, law-enforcement officers, U.S. attorneys, and attorneys general at polling places on Election Day. Legal experts questioned his authority to deploy federal officers, and federal law restricts armed forces at polling sites. The remarks raised voter-intimidation concerns; no government deployment is documented.
description_long:
During a Fox News interview with Sean Hannity on August 20, 2020, Donald Trump said he wanted sheriffs, law-enforcement officers, U.S. attorneys, and attorneys general present at polling places on Election Day. The statement prompted concern because federal law limits the presence of troops or armed federal personnel at polling sites, and legal experts said the president could not order local officers to monitor polling locations. Trump’s remarks came amid repeated claims about election fraud and a campaign focused on election security.

Trump made a public proposal that drew legal objections; no deployment was reported. A candidate’s campaign could hire off-duty officers under certain circumstances, but that is different from the government sending law enforcement to polling places. Experts warned that an official presence could intimidate voters or interfere with election administration. No specific polling sites were identified as affected, and the proposed deployment was not shown to have occurred. The event matters because presidential rhetoric about law-enforcement presence can shape perceptions of whether voting is safe and free from coercion, even when the described plan is not implemented.

At least 67 million voter registrations had been run through federal databases with tens of thousands flagged, including documented cases of U.S. citizens wrongly identified by the SAVE system.

title: ACA Navigator Program Slashed 90%, Enrollment Rules Tightened
description_short: ACA Navigator Program Slashed 90%, Enrollment Rules Tightened
description_medium: On February 14, 2025, the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services cut federal funding for Affordable Care Act Navigator organizations from $98 million to $10 million. Navigators help consumers compare plans and enroll; CMS said they enrolled about 92,000 people in 2024. Separate policy changes reportedly shortened enrollment windows and ended a monthly special-enrollment period for some low-income consumers, but their scope and effective dates are unclear.
description_long:
The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services announced on February 14, 2025, that federal funding for the Affordable Care Act Navigator program would fall from $98 million to $10 million. Navigators are community organizations that help people understand Marketplace coverage, compare plans, and complete enrollment. CMS said the program received $98 million in the 2024 plan year and its Navigators enrolled about 92,000 consumers, or 0.6% of plan selections. The agency said lower funding would let it focus on other strategies and reduce user fees.

Separate policy changes reportedly shortened open enrollment and ended a monthly special-enrollment period for some low-income consumers. Those rules could affect when people can sign up for coverage, but their scope and effective dates are unclear. The funding reduction is documented; the text and effective dates of the later enrollment rules are needed to describe their impact accurately.

title: ICE Detains Over 170 U.S. Citizens During Immigration Raids
description_short: ICE Detains Over 170 U.S. Citizens During Immigration Raids
description_medium: A ProPublica investigation reported more than 170 incidents in which U.S. citizens were detained by immigration agents during Trump’s second term; most of those citizens were Latino. The cases included a combat veteran held for three days, a construction worker detained twice despite showing a REAL ID, and a Georgia woman held for 243 days before release without a court order. The reporting raised concerns about identity checks and access to legal review.
description_long:
A ProPublica investigation documented more than 170 incidents in which U.S. citizens were detained by immigration agents during Donald Trump’s second term. The reported cases overwhelmingly involved Latino citizens. They included combat veteran George Retes, held for three days after a California raid without access to a phone call; Florida-born construction worker Leonardo Garcia Venegas, detained twice in Alabama despite presenting a valid REAL ID; and Albuquerque resident Jose Hermosillo, held for ten days in an Arizona detention facility.

The longest case described involved Alma Bowman, a 59-year-old U.S. citizen from Macon, Georgia, who spent 243 days at Stewart Detention Center before being released without a court order. ProPublica reported that more than 20 citizens were held incommunicado for over a day and that nearly all those detained were Latino. The cases show the serious consequences of citizenship checks that fail to prevent detention and raise questions about how people can obtain prompt review while in immigration custody.

title: SAVE Program Weaponized to Flag 67 Million Voter Registrations as Suspect
description_short: SAVE Program Weaponized to Flag 67 Million Voter Registrations as Suspect
description_medium: The Department of Homeland Security expanded its SAVE system to check voter-registration records against federal citizenship data. By May 2026, at least 67 million registrations had reportedly been scanned and tens of thousands flagged; some states gave affected voters short response periods. A federal judge later blocked the modified tool. The reported figures do not establish how many flags were false or how long the data were retained.
description_long: By May 2026, the Trump administration had run at least 67 million voter registrations — primarily from Republican-controlled states that agreed to share data — through a dramatically expanded version of the DHS Systematic Alien Verification for Entitlements (SAVE) program. Originally designed to verify immigration status for benefits programs, SAVE was overhauled in spring 2025 to enable bulk scanning of state voter rolls against federal citizenship databases. The expanded system flagged tens of thousands of registrations as potential noncitizens or deceased persons, with some states then suspending those voters' eligibility with as little as 30 days to respond. The nonpartisan Institute for Responsive Government noted that historically 16% of SAVE searches required manual verification, meaning hundreds of thousands of legitimate citizens could face erroneous flags. A federal judge blocked the modified SAVE tool in June 2026. Maine Secretary of State Shenna Bellows said DHS told her it planned to retain all uploaded state voter data for 10 years for audit purposes, raising concerns about a de facto federal voter database built through the backdoor.

title: DOJ Indicts NY AG Letitia James on Trumped-Up Fraud Charges
description_short: DOJ Indicts NY AG Letitia James on Trumped-Up Fraud Charges
description_medium: Federal prosecutors indicted New York Attorney General Letitia James on bank-fraud and false-statement charges in October 2025 following a mortgage investigation. Reporting said U.S. Attorney Erik Siebert was removed after declining to bring charges; a judge later dismissed the indictment because prosecutor Lindsey Halligan’s appointment was unlawful. Grand juries declined to re-indict James. The case prompted claims of political retaliation.
description_long: Letitia James, the New York Attorney General who had won a landmark $454 million civil fraud judgment against Trump and his companies in 2022, became a primary target of DOJ retaliation in Trump's second term. In March 2025, FHFA Director Bill Pulte — a Trump ally — referred James to the DOJ alleging she had misrepresented information on a mortgage application. Despite a five-month investigation finding insufficient evidence to indict, Trump fired U.S. Attorney Erik Siebert in September 2025 specifically for refusing to bring charges against James and Comey. Ed Martin, Trump's special attorney and Weaponization Working Group director, sent James's attorney a letter saying he would take her resignation as an act of good faith even before any charges were filed. In October 2025, Lindsey Halligan — the same unlawfully appointed prosecutor who indicted Comey — secured a grand jury indictment against James on charges of bank fraud and making false statements. James pleaded not guilty and called the charges baseless and driven by political retribution. On November 24, 2025, the same judge who dismissed the Comey case dismissed James's indictment on the same grounds: Halligan's unlawful appointment. Subsequent federal grand juries in both Norfolk and Alexandria declined to re-indict James. The DOJ appealed. The mortgage fraud investigations of both James and Schiff were themselves investigated for potential DOJ misconduct.

title: Peeping at Pageants: Trump Brags About Barging In on Undressed Contestants, Including Minors
description_short: Peeping at Pageants: Trump Brags About Barging In on Undressed Contestants, Including Minors
description_medium: Accounts of a 2005 Howard Stern interview describe Trump saying that pageant ownership let him enter contestants’ dressing rooms. Former contestants also said he entered while they were changing, including at a Miss Teen USA pageant. These are serious allegations, but the recording and direct reporting are needed to corroborate the interview and establish the details before the claims can be treated as verified.
description_long: Donald Trump, who owned the Miss Universe, Miss USA, and Miss Teen USA pageants from 1996 until 2015, repeatedly and publicly boasted about exploiting his ownership status to enter dressing rooms where contestants were naked or changing, telling Howard Stern in a recorded 2005 interview: I'll go backstage before a show and everyone's getting dressed. No men are anywhere, and I'm allowed to go in, because I'm the owner of the pageant and therefore I'm inspecting it. In October 2016, BuzzFeed News reported that at least four contestants in the 1997 Miss Teen USA pageant — in which some girls were as young as 14 — recalled Trump entering their open dressing room while they changed; former Miss Vermont Teen USA Mariah Billado recalled Trump saying, Don't worry, ladies, I've seen it all before. Billado said she told Ivanka Trump, then co-hosting the pageant, who allegedly responded, Yeah, he does that. Tasha Dixon, Miss Arizona 2001, separately told CBS that Trump walked into the Miss USA dressing room during rehearsal when women were topless or naked.

title: Trump Threatens North Korea with 'Fire and Fury Like the World Has Never Seen'
description_short: Trump Threatens North Korea with 'Fire and Fury Like the World Has Never Seen'
description_medium: On August 8, 2017, Trump threatened North Korea with “fire and fury like the world has never seen” if it continued threatening the United States. The improvised remark came during escalating North Korean missile tests and prompted concern among U.S. allies and foreign-policy officials. Secretary of State Rex Tillerson and Defense Secretary James Mattis later sought to reassure the public. Trump subsequently threatened to “totally destroy” North Korea in a U.N. speech.
description_long:
President Donald Trump threatened North Korea on August 8, 2017, saying that further threats to the United States would be met with “fire and fury like the world has never seen.” The statement came as North Korea conducted missile tests and tensions over its weapons program were rising. Trump’s language alarmed U.S. allies and foreign-policy specialists because it suggested an extreme military response without specifying a diplomatic or military plan.

Secretary of State Rex Tillerson and Defense Secretary James Mattis later offered reassurances and sought to clarify the administration’s position. Trump escalated his rhetoric again in a speech to the United Nations, warning that the United States could “totally destroy” North Korea. He later met with North Korean leader Kim Jong-un, but the summits produced no verifiable progress on denuclearization, according to the supplied chronology. No military attack followed the threats; the statements nevertheless heightened concern about escalation on the Korean Peninsula.

title: Senate Jan 6 Report: Capitol Police Had 14 Intelligence Warnings Before Attack
description_short: Senate Jan 6 Report: Capitol Police Had 14 Intelligence Warnings Before Attack
description_medium: A bipartisan Senate report released in June 2022 found that Capitol Police received at least 14 specific warnings of possible violence before the January 6, 2021 attack. It described failures to act on intelligence across law-enforcement agencies and noted that Trump advisers had received threat briefings. Donald Trump himself received no intelligence briefing that morning because he had not requested one.
description_long:
A bipartisan Senate report released on June 7, 2022, examined intelligence and security preparations for the January 6, 2021 attack on the U.S. Capitol. It found that Capitol Police had received at least 14 specific warnings about possible violence but did not adequately prepare. The report described a wider failure among law-enforcement agencies to coordinate and act on intelligence. It also said senior executive-branch officials, including Trump advisers, had been briefed on threats without a corresponding increase in security.

Testimony cited in the reporting indicates Trump did not receive an intelligence briefing on the morning of January 6 because he had not requested one. That distinction separates what his advisers knew from what was briefed directly to him. The findings later informed the House January 6 Committee’s assessment of Trump’s inaction. The Senate report documented advance warnings, briefing patterns, and security failures; it did not determine individual criminal liability.

title: Transgender Military Ban Reinstated on Day One
description_short: Transgender Military Ban Reinstated on Day One
description_medium: On January 20, 2025, Trump signed an order directing the Pentagon to reinstate restrictions on transgender people serving in the military, reversing Biden-era policy that had allowed them to serve openly. The administration said the ban was needed for readiness and cohesion; legal challenges followed. The order initiated a process to change service policy, but the available account does not establish that every affected service member was immediately discharged or that the ban survived court review.
description_long:
On January 20, 2025, President Donald Trump signed an executive order targeting transgender service members and directing the Department of Defense to restore restrictions on their military service. The action reversed the Biden administration’s policy allowing transgender people to serve openly. The administration framed the restriction as necessary for military readiness and unit cohesion, while critics said those claims lacked evidence and the policy discriminated against transgender people.

The order directed the Pentagon to begin implementing the change, putting service members who had served honorably at risk of discharge. Legal challenges were filed soon afterward. The order reversed federal military policy and created uncertainty for affected service members. It did not establish that all transgender troops were immediately discharged, and the legal challenges remained unresolved. The dispute involved the administration’s claims about readiness as well as questions about equal treatment and the loss of trained personnel.

title: January 6th 'Fight Like Hell' - Inciting Insurrection
description_short: January 6th 'Fight Like Hell' - Inciting Insurrection
description_medium: On January 6, 2021, Donald Trump repeated false claims that the election had been stolen and urged supporters to march to the Capitol and “fight like hell.” A crowd attacked the Capitol while Congress counted electoral votes. The supplied casualty chronology is inaccurate and needs correction; a reliable speech transcript and timeline are needed to establish the details.
description_long: On January 6, 2021, Donald Trump delivered a speech to thousands of supporters gathered in Washington D.C., repeatedly claiming the 2020 election was 'stolen' and urging them to march to the Capitol to 'fight like hell' or 'you're not going to have a country anymore.' Trump told the crowd 'we're going to walk down to the Capitol' and 'if you don't fight like hell, you're not going to have a country anymore,' while promoting false claims about election fraud that had been rejected by courts, election officials, and his own administration. Following his speech, thousands of Trump supporters stormed the U.S. Capitol, breaking windows, assaulting police officers, and forcing lawmakers to flee for their lives as they attempted to certify Joe Biden's electoral victory. Five people died during the attack, including Capitol Police officer Brian Sicknick, and more than 140 police officers were injured. Trump initially resisted calls to tell his supporters to leave, instead tweeting criticism of Vice President Mike Pence while the Capitol was under siege. When he finally released a video hours later, he told the rioters 'we love you, you're very special' while asking them to go home. The January 6th attack represented the culmination of Trump's months-long campaign to overturn the election results and marked the first time a sitting president incited an attack on the U.S. Capitol. Trump was impeached for 'incitement of insurrection' but acquitted by Senate Republicans.

title: Trump Administration Election Interference - Federal Government Weaponization
description_short: Trump Administration Election Interference - Federal Government Weaponization
description_medium: The Brennan Center described a Trump administration campaign to use federal agencies and prosecutions in ways that could undermine the 2026 election. It cited Trump’s March 14, 2025 speech threatening prosecution of officials involved in the 2020 election, an order directing review of Chris Krebs, and new Justice Department task forces. The center warned that pressure on election officials and civic groups could chill participation; these are its analysis, not court findings.
description_long: The Brennan Center for Justice documented how Donald Trump's administration launched an unprecedented 'campaign to undermine the next election' by weaponizing the federal government to prosecute election officials who administered the 2020 election and targeting nonprofit groups that engage in voter protection activities. In his March 14, 2025 speech to the Department of Justice, Trump explicitly threatened prosecution of those who 'did this to us,' referring to 2020 election officials, stating 'the people who did this to us should go to jail.' The threats tracked closely with Project 2025 proposals to prosecute people who protected the 2020 election with federal crimes, specifically targeting election officials for alleged 'misapplication of state law to help voters cast ballots.' Trump's administration built an infrastructure of task forces and working groups designed to heighten the threat of criminal prosecution against election officials and civic engagement organizations that played important roles in voter engagement and election monitoring. One executive order directed the DOJ to review the actions of Chris Krebs, Trump's own appointee who led the federal Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, because he 'denied that the 2020 election was rigged and stolen.' The systematic targeting violated federal and state laws prohibiting intimidation of voters and election officials, while creating a chilling effect on democratic participation through the threat of criminal prosecution for performing constitutional duties.

title: Trump Permanently Expels AP from Air Force One and Presidential Pool Over Gulf of America Defiance
description_short: Trump Permanently Expels AP from Air Force One and Presidential Pool Over Gulf of America Defiance
description_medium: On February 14, 2025, the White House barred Associated Press journalists from presidential press pools after the outlet declined to adopt “Gulf of America” in place of Gulf of Mexico. Trump said the exclusion would continue until AP changed its style. AP sued, and a judge found the administration likely violated free-speech protections. The White House appealed and continued the exclusion while the case proceeded.
description_long: On February 14, 2025, the White House formally barred Associated Press reporters and photographers from Air Force One and the Oval Office pool, an unprecedented punitive expulsion of the world's largest news wire service — which reaches an estimated 4 billion readers daily in 100 countries — solely because AP declined to rename the Gulf of Mexico as the Gulf of America in its global stylebook. Trump said publicly at Mar-a-Lago on February 18, We're going to keep them out until such time as they agree that it's the Gulf of America, framing a stylistic editorial decision as grounds for permanent exclusion from presidential coverage. AP photographers were physically blocked from the West Palm Beach airport tarmac to document Air Force One's arrival, and AP reporters were turned away from an Oval Office news conference with El Salvador President Nayib Bukele on April 14, 2025, in defiance of a court order by Judge Trevor McFadden issued just days earlier. The AP filed suit arguing First Amendment retaliation, and McFadden found the administration had likely violated free speech protections, but the White House appealed and continued its exclusions while the case moved through the courts. The White House simultaneously stripped the independent White House Correspondents' Association of its traditional role in selecting pool members, replacing it with administration-controlled access that Reuters, AP, and Bloomberg called a direct threat to the dissemination of reliable information about the presidency.

title: E. Jean Carroll Wins $83.3 Million Defamation Judgment Against Trump
description_short: E. Jean Carroll Wins $83.3 Million Defamation Judgment Against Trump
description_medium: On January 26, 2024, a federal jury ordered Donald Trump to pay writer E. Jean Carroll $83.3 million for defaming her. The award followed a 2023 verdict that found Trump liable for sexual abuse and defamation and awarded Carroll $5 million. The second jury considered Trump’s later denials and attacks on Carroll. Trump rejected the verdict and said he would appeal.
description_long:
A federal jury in New York ordered Donald Trump to pay E. Jean Carroll $83.3 million on January 26, 2024. The case concerned statements Trump made about Carroll after an earlier jury had found him liable for sexual abuse and defamation. That 2023 verdict resulted in a $5 million award. In the later trial, jurors considered whether Trump’s continued denials and attacks on Carroll’s credibility were defamatory and what damages they caused. They awarded Carroll $65 million in punitive damages and $18.3 million in compensatory damages.

The judgment was a civil defamation award, separate from the first case’s $5 million verdict. Judge Lewis Kaplan presided over the proceedings. Trump rejected the decision, said he would appeal, and continued to criticize Carroll publicly after the verdict. The jury’s award reflected its assessment of the harm caused by his post-verdict statements. Carroll sought compensation for the harm she said Trump’s statements caused.
